claims.text: Powder-based ceramics traditionally require high-temperature sintering to achieve densification.
Advanced free-energy simulation methods can be used to study thermally activated materials processes.
Metadynamics or related free-energy sampling can map the free-energy landscape of ceramic sintering and identify critical energy barriers.
Simulation results can guide the selection of sintering aids or dopants that lower the identified barriers.
Atomic-scale diffusion and rearrangement at grain boundaries and interparticle interfaces are governed by the identified energy barriers.
Tailored additives or dopants can reduce barriers associated with atomic diffusion and particle bonding during ceramic sintering.
Reducing kinetic barriers to diffusion and particle bonding lowers the thermodynamic driving force required for densification.
Lowering the relevant energy barriers permits effective densification at a lower sintering temperature.
Simulation-guided interventions will significantly reduce the required sintering temperature while retaining or improving densification and microstructure.
High energy barriers necessitate elevated temperatures in conventional ceramic sintering.
The proposed strategy is specifically applicable to powder-based ceramics.
Application of the strategy to complex or multiphase systems requires further validation.
The achievable temperature reduction depends on material composition, processing environment, and intervention effectiveness.
The exact magnitude of the temperature reduction is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The low-temperature arm may use an optimized dopant profile, but the experiment also says the two sets are otherwise identical except for their temperature profiles. Adding or changing dopants introduces an additional experimental difference.
